title: Iraq
hookLine: the Jews of Iraq, descendants of the Babylonian exile, from the rivers of Babylon to the streets of Baghdad

cards: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." That line from the Psalms is sung by people who have never seen those rivers. But some Jews did not just sing about Babylon.

They stayed there. Their families lived beside the Tigris and the Euphrates, in the land we now call Iraq, from the exile onward. Today, a community that began in tears and went on to build something lasting.

teach.b: The Tanakh tells how the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and carried many of its people away to Babylon. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven is their grief.
But the book of Ezekiel opens in the same land, with a surprise. The prophet is not in the Temple.

teach.h: THE HEAVENS OPEN BY THE CHEBAR.
teach.b: He is in Babylon, beside a river, and he says so plainly: "as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God." The Temple was far away, and the heavens opened anyway.
When the Persians later allowed a return to Jerusalem, some went home. Others stayed. That community grew into a great center of Jewish learning.

In its academies the rabbis argued and taught for generations, and their discussions became the Babylonian Talmud. So a text studied in yeshivas today was shaped beside the same rivers where the exiles once wept.
Later, under the caliphs, Baghdad rose nearby, and Jewish life moved into its streets: scholars, merchants, families, synagogues, and a Judeo-Arabic way of speaking all their own.
Then, after hard and frightening years, the community left, much of it for Israel.
A very old story, from Babylon to Baghdad, almost closed in one lifetime. Still, its Talmud, its melodies and its recipes go on wherever its children live.

how: Jews of Iraqi descent keep Babylonian Jewish customs and melodies in their synagogues and homes, and Jewish students everywhere study the Babylonian Talmud that took shape in Iraq's academies.

games.q: you are among the exiles in Babylon, beside the river Chebar. where does the book of Ezekiel say the heavens opened?
o: right there, by the river Chebar.
games.why: "as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, that the heavens were opened": the vision came in exile, far from the Temple.

practice: Picture a riverbank, and people sitting there far from home. Then the same riverbank generations later: houses, gardens, a room full of students arguing over a page.
Hold both, the grief and the life that grew after it, and if you pray, remember the Jews of Iraq in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Iraq. The land of ancient Babylon, where Jewish exiles settled, where the Babylonian Talmud took shape, and where Jews later lived in Baghdad. Today's word.

orig.note: Babylon in Hebrew; the Babylonian Talmud is called the Talmud Bavli.

carryVoice: Your line: babylon to baghdad. The heavens opened beside a foreign river. That's day nine hundred eighty-one.
